en.title: Human Resource Management: the whole course
en.short: What an HRM degree or diploma covers, how it is organised, and how to study it well.

sections.heading: What human resource management is
sections.text:
Human resource management (HRM) is the management of people at work, so that the organisation reaches its goals and the people are treated fairly. It covers the whole employment relationship: deciding how many people and what skills are needed, attracting and choosing them, paying them, training them, keeping them safe, and handling disagreement.

It is both a set of activities and a way of thinking. The activities are familiar: recruitment, appraisal, payroll, training, discipline. The way of thinking, which became prominent in the 1980s, argues that people can be a source of competitive advantage and should be managed in line with strategy rather than treated as a cost to be cut. Critics reply that this can be rhetoric that hides longer hours and less secure work. That argument is part of the subject, not a distraction from it.

sections.heading: How the course is usually organised
sections.text:
Lengths, awards and module names differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook. Some common patterns: in Nigeria a full-time BSc is often four years, including a period of industrial work experience, and HND programmes run through ND and HND stages. In the UK a bachelor’s degree is usually three years, often four with a placement year. In Ghana four years is common; in South Africa a three-year BCom is often followed by an honours year.

Professional bodies sit alongside the degrees: CIPM in Nigeria, CIPD in the UK, SHRM (US-based, with members worldwide) and AHRI in Australia. Some degrees carry exemptions from parts of a professional qualification. The rules change, so confirm directly with the body.

A master’s degree, such as an MSc in HRM or an MBA, adds theory and research training and usually ends with a dissertation.

sections.heading: The main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
The course starts with foundations borrowed from other disciplines: principles of management, organisational behaviour, labour market economics, business statistics, the basics of employment law, communication skills, finance and accounting, and business ethics.

The core then follows the employment cycle: strategy and workforce planning, job analysis and design, recruitment and selection, onboarding, engagement and retention, learning and development, performance management, and reward. Around these sit employee relations and industrial relations, applied employment law, health, safety and wellbeing, diversity, equity and inclusion, talent management and career development, HR analytics and information systems, international and comparative HRM, professional ethics, and research methods.

At master’s level you meet advanced HRM theory, advanced research methods for a dissertation, people analytics and artificial intelligence, and sustainable HRM and decent work.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Anchor each topic to the employment cycle. Ask where it sits: before someone joins, while they work, or when they leave. Then ask what problem it solves and what it costs.

Use one organisation as a running case, real or invented, and apply every new idea to it. A small firm with thirty staff and a large bank will need different answers.

Separate three questions that students often merge: what the law requires, what the organisation chooses to do, and what the evidence says works. Law is national, so name the country. Evidence comes from research, so name the study or say plainly that you are reasoning from principle. For the quantitative topics, practise the calculations by hand. For essay topics, write a plan before you write the answer.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
The most common error is to treat HRM as only soft skills. Selection, reward and analytics all involve measurement, cost and evidence.

Other frequent mistakes:
Assuming one country’s employment law applies everywhere. Nigeria’s Labour Act and the National Industrial Court are not the same as the UK’s Employment Rights Act 1996 and its employment tribunals.
Describing a practice without saying why it should work or what evidence supports it.
Quoting a statistic with no source, or a figure that has changed since the textbook was printed.
Ignoring cost. Every proposal has a budget.
Confusing HRM with old-style personnel management without knowing what changed and what did not.

keyPoints: HRM covers the whole employment relationship, from workforce planning to exit.
It is both a set of activities and a strategic way of thinking about people.
Degree length and award differ by country, so check your own handbook.
Employment law is national: always name the country whose rules you are describing.
Separate what the law requires, what the employer chooses and what evidence supports.
Practise the quantitative parts by hand and plan essays before writing them.

en.title: Introduction to Human Resource Management
en.short: HRM definitions, functions, evolution, the HRM cycle, stakeholders, strategy and the psychological contract.

sections.heading: What HRM is
sections.text:
Human resource management (HRM) is managing people at work so that individual and organisational goals are met. Its functions include workforce planning, recruitment and selection, learning, performance, reward, employee relations, health and safety, and people records.

HR roles range from administrative and advisory to strategic. Personnel management, the earlier name, was mainly administrative: hiring, pay records, welfare and compliance. From the late twentieth century, HRM stressed strategy, commitment and competitive advantage. The change was uneven; many organisations combine both approaches.

sections.heading: Cycle and stakeholders
sections.text:
The HRM cycle links people activities in a loop: plan needs, attract and select, develop, reward and retain, then manage exit. Stakeholders differ. Employees want fair pay, voice, safety and security. Managers want performance; owners want results. Unions represent members; customers and society expect lawful, decent treatment.

These expectations conflict, so HR balances them through policy, dialogue and evidence. In an Accra delivery firm, riders ask for higher pay, managers want lower costs and customers want reliable service; HR must explain the trade-offs and apply consistent rules.

sections.heading: Operational and strategic
sections.text:
Operational HR is day-to-day work: contracts, payroll queries, records, absence and compliance. Strategic people management looks ahead and aligns people with long-term goals, culture, talent and change. The same task can be either.

Filling one vacancy is operational; building a skills pipeline for a new market is strategic. Strategic HRM depends on reliable operational HR, because poor records and late pay undermine trust.

sections.heading: Models and contract
sections.text:
Debate continues over HRM models. Universalist or best-practice views claim practices raise performance everywhere. Contingency or best-fit views say practices must match strategy, culture and law. Soft HRM stresses commitment and development; hard HRM treats people as a resource to use efficiently. No model is proven best in all settings.

The psychological contract is the unwritten beliefs about what employee and employer owe each other. Transactional contracts exchange pay for work; relational contracts add trust, development and security. Breach, such as broken promotion promises, can reduce commitment and increase turnover.

keyPoints: HRM manages people to meet individual and organisational goals through functions such as planning, recruitment, development, reward and employee relations.
Personnel management was mainly administrative, while HRM added a strategic and commitment focus.
The HRM cycle links planning, attracting, developing, rewarding, retaining and exit.
Stakeholders have conflicting expectations, so HR balances them through policy, dialogue and evidence.
Operational HR handles day-to-day administration; strategic HR aligns people with long-term goals.
Debate over best practice and best fit, and soft and hard HRM, shows no single model fits all; the psychological contract is unwritten mutual expectation, and breach reduces trust.

en.title: Principles of Management for HRM
en.short: The four management functions, structure, authority, delegation, coordination, manager roles and basic decisions.

sections.heading: The four functions
sections.text: Management is often described through four functions. Planning sets goals and decides in advance how to reach them. Organising arranges work, people and resources into roles and units. Leading guides and motivates people to do the work. Controlling compares actual results with plans, then corrects gaps. In HRM, these functions shape how people are grouped, directed and reviewed.

sections.heading: Structure and authority
sections.text: Organisational structure is the pattern of roles, reporting lines and units. Functional structure groups by specialism; divisional by product, service or region; matrix combines both and creates dual reporting. Authority is the right to give instructions. Responsibility is the duty to perform work. Delegation passes authority to a subordinate, but accountability for the final result stays with the manager. Span of control is number of direct reports. Narrow spans mean closer supervision but more layers. Coordination is aligning different people and units so they pull together, through plans, meetings, clear roles and information systems.

sections.heading: Manager and decisions
sections.text: A manager plans, organises, leads and controls, and also represents the unit, gathers information and handles disturbances. Henry Mintzberg described roles such as figurehead, leader, liaison, monitor, spokesperson, resource allocator and negotiator. Decision making is choosing among options. A simple sequence: define the problem, gather relevant information, list options, weigh costs and benefits, choose, implement, then review the result. Good decisions fit the organisation’s goals and are recorded so they can be checked.

sections.heading: Case: Amina’s kitchen
sections.text: Amina manages a 40-person catering firm in Kano, Nigeria. She plans weekly menus and delivery targets. She organises staff into kitchen, packing and delivery teams, and delegates shift rosters to three supervisors. She leads through daily briefings and controls by checking waste, late deliveries and customer complaints. When complaints rise, she defines the problem, compares three options, chooses extra packing checks, and reviews the result after two weeks. Delegation frees her for planning, while accountability for service quality remains with her.

keyPoints: Planning sets goals and means; organising arranges work and resources; leading guides people; controlling compares results with plans.
Structure groups roles and reporting lines; functional, divisional and matrix forms are common.
Authority is the right to instruct, responsibility is the duty to act, and accountability for the final result cannot be delegated.
Delegation passes authority to a subordinate and should include a clear task, resources and deadline.
Coordination aligns units through plans, meetings, clear roles and information.
Basic decision making defines the problem, compares options, chooses, implements and reviews.

en.title: Organisational Behaviour Foundations
en.short: Individual differences, motivation, groups, culture, power and politics, and how HR practice uses them.

sections.heading: Individual differences
sections.text: Organisational behaviour studies how people think, feel and act at work. Individual differences are stable variations in personality, ability, values and self-efficacy, the belief in one’s capacity to succeed. Perception and attitudes also shape behaviour, so two employees may interpret the same comment differently. HR practice uses this by avoiding one-size-fits-all policies, checking person-job fit and matching support or training to the person.

sections.heading: Motivation theories
sections.text: Motivation is the force that starts, directs and sustains effort. Content theories ask what people need, and include Maslow’s hierarchy and Herzberg’s two-factor theory. Herzberg separates hygiene factors, such as pay and conditions, from motivators. Process theories ask how motivation works: expectancy theory says effort depends on expected performance and valued outcomes; equity theory says people compare their input-outcome ratio with others; goal-setting theory says specific, challenging goals with feedback raise performance. HR practice links these to fair reward, feedback and job design.

sections.heading: Groups and teams
sections.text: A group is two or more people who interact and influence one another. Group dynamics include norms, roles and cohesiveness. Norms are shared rules of behaviour; roles are expected patterns of conduct. Cohesiveness can improve performance but may encourage conformity. Social loafing is reduced effort in a group. Tuckman’s model describes team development as forming, storming, norming, performing and adjourning. HR practice uses this in team composition, clear roles and time for conflict. Case: at a made-up Lagos firm, Ada, Tunde, Halima and Chidi argued over duties in week one. The supervisor clarified roles and set targets; by week six they performed steadily.

sections.heading: Culture, power, politics
sections.text: Organisational culture is the shared values, beliefs and assumptions that guide behaviour. Schein describes visible artefacts, espoused values (the values an organisation says it holds) and deeper assumptions. Power is the capacity to influence others. French and Raven identify legitimate, reward, coercive, expert and referent power. Organisational politics is the use of influence for personal or group interests. HR practice shapes culture through what it rewards, trains managers to use power fairly and designs transparent procedures to limit destructive politics.

keyPoints: Individual differences mean HR should avoid one-size-fits-all policies and check person-job fit.
Motivation theories divide into content theories about needs and process theories about how effort is directed.
Expectancy, equity and goal-setting theories link motivation to expected outcomes, fairness and specific feedback.
Group norms, roles and cohesiveness shape behaviour, and Tuckman’s stages describe team development.
Organisational culture is shared values and assumptions; power bases include legitimate, reward, coercive, expert and referent power.
Organisational politics can help or harm, so HR should reward desired culture and use transparent procedures.

en.title: Labour Market Economics
en.short: Labour demand and supply, wages, human capital, unemployment and mobility for HR decisions.

sections.heading: Demand and supply
sections.text: Labour demand is derived demand: firms hire workers because they help produce output. In theory a firm hires until marginal revenue product (MRP), the extra revenue from one more worker, equals the wage. MRP equals marginal product multiplied by output price. Labour supply is the number willing to offer time at each wage. It depends on pay, conditions, skills, migration and alternatives. The market wage tends to settle where demand meets supply, but minimum wages, unions, bargaining and taxes can change it. These institutions differ by country.

sections.heading: Human capital
sections.text: Human capital is the skills, knowledge and health that people carry. Education and training can raise productivity and so can raise pay. General training is useful to many employers; firm-specific training is useful mainly to the current employer. Employers use qualifications and experience as signals when recruiting, but they should test skills rather than assume. Pay also reflects scarcity, productivity, comparability with other employers and local institutions.

sections.heading: Unemployment and mobility
sections.text: Unemployment has several types. Frictional unemployment is the short gap while people search for work. Structural unemployment is a mismatch between skills or locations and available jobs. Cyclical unemployment rises when demand in the economy falls. Seasonal unemployment follows regular changes in work. Labour mobility is movement between jobs, occupations or places. Occupational mobility needs transferable skills; geographic mobility needs affordable housing, family support and recognition of qualifications. Barriers reduce the pool of candidates and can push wages up in shortage areas.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A made-up firm adds one worker producing 20 units a day, sold at 500 naira each. MRP is 20 × 500 = 10,000 naira daily. At a wage of 8,000, hiring adds 2,000 daily, so the firm hires. If price falls to 300, MRP is 20 × 300 = 6,000, below the wage, so it does not. HR uses this logic in recruitment and pay. Workforce planning compares local supply, unemployment and mobility with future demand. Check official data and laws, which vary by country.

keyPoints: Labour demand is derived demand; hire while marginal revenue product is at least the wage.
Marginal revenue product = marginal product × output price.
Wages are shaped by supply and demand and by institutions such as minimum wages, unions and bargaining.
Human capital is skills, knowledge and health; training can raise productivity and pay.
Unemployment includes frictional, structural, cyclical and seasonal types; mobility can be occupational or geographic.
Recruitment, pay and workforce planning should use current local labour data and laws, which vary by country.

en.title: Business Statistics for HRM
en.short: Summarising HR data, sampling, confidence intervals and basic tests, with interpretation.

sections.heading: Describing HR data
sections.text: Descriptive statistics summarise a set of numbers. The mean is the total divided by the count. The median is the middle value when ordered. The standard deviation measures spread around the mean. HR often uses rates: turnover rate = leavers ÷ average headcount × 100; absence rate = days absent ÷ possible days × 100. Compare rates across departments or years, not raw counts, because department sizes differ. A high turnover rate may reflect pay, management or seasonal work; the number alone does not explain why.

sections.heading: Sampling and probability
sections.text: A population is everyone you want to describe; a sample is the part you measure. Random sampling gives every member a known chance of selection and reduces bias. Probability is the long-run chance of an event, from 0 to 1. It underlies sampling: a 95% confidence interval uses the spread of sample means. Non-random samples, such as volunteers, can mislead. Non-response and missing records are common HR problems.

sections.heading: Confidence intervals
sections.text: A confidence interval gives a range likely to contain the population value. For a mean, it is sample mean ± z × standard error, where standard error = standard deviation ÷ √n. For 95% confidence, z is about 1.96. Example: 100 employees have mean pay 120,000 naira and standard deviation 20,000. Standard error = 20,000 ÷ √100 = 2,000. Interval = 120,000 ± 1.96 × 2,000 = 116,080 to 123,920 naira. Wider intervals mean more uncertainty; larger samples narrow them.

sections.heading: Testing claims
sections.text: A hypothesis test asks whether data support a claim. The null hypothesis usually says there is no difference or no effect. The p-value is the chance of a result at least as extreme if the null is true. A small p-value, often below 0.05, is called statistically significant. This does not prove a large or important effect. Tests assume random samples and suitable data. Always report the size of the difference and check whether the sample is representative.

keyPoints: Mean = sum of values ÷ count; median = middle ordered value; standard deviation measures spread.
Turnover rate = leavers ÷ average headcount × 100; absence rate = days absent ÷ possible days × 100.
Standard error = standard deviation ÷ √n; a 95% confidence interval is about mean ± 1.96 × standard error.
A p-value is the probability of the observed result, or a more extreme one, if the null hypothesis is true.
Statistical significance is not practical importance; report the size of the difference.
Random sampling reduces bias; non-random samples and missing data limit conclusions.

en.title: Employment Law Foundations
en.short: Sources of employment law, the contract, basic rights and duties, and dispute bodies.

sections.heading: Sources of employment law
sections.text: Employment law comes from several sources. A constitution sets fundamental rights. Statutes, such as Nigeria’s Labour Act, set minimum terms on wages, hours, leave and notice. Common law supplies implied duties from court decisions. Collective agreements between unions and employers can bind their parties, especially when they are incorporated into individual contracts. Ratified international labour standards and codes also influence practice. Nigeria is the illustration here, but every country has its own mix, so check the current national law.

sections.heading: Contract of employment
sections.text: The contract of employment is the legal basis of the relationship. It begins with offer and acceptance, and it needs consideration (pay), capacity and lawful purpose. Terms may be express, such as job title and salary, or implied, such as honesty and reasonable care. Statute can override a contract term. In Nigeria, many workers must receive written particulars of their main terms. HR must keep contracts accurate and apply them consistently.

sections.heading: Rights, duties and HR limits
sections.text: Basic rights and duties flow from the contract and statute. Employers must pay agreed wages, provide a safe workplace and treat employees with dignity. Employees must work with care, obey lawful instructions, keep confidences and act loyally. Law constrains HR decisions: recruitment, discipline, pay cuts and dismissal must follow the contract, statute and fair procedure. HR cannot treat a legal minimum as optional.

sections.heading: Disputes and a case
sections.text: Disputes may go first to internal grievance procedures, then to conciliation or arbitration. In Nigeria, the National Industrial Court hears labour disputes, and the Industrial Arbitration Panel handles some arbitration. A case: Amina, an HR manager in Lagos, wants a 20% pay cut. The contracts set wages, so she must consult and negotiate; a unilateral cut may breach the contract. If talks fail, the dispute can go to conciliation and then the court. Rules differ by country.

keyPoints: Employment law comes from constitution, statutes, common law, collective agreements and international standards.
The contract of employment is built on offer, acceptance, consideration and lawful purpose.
Statute can override a contract term, so HR must apply the higher legal minimum.
Employers owe wages, safety and dignity; employees owe care, obedience and loyalty.
HR decisions on pay, discipline and dismissal must follow the contract and fair procedure.
Dispute bodies differ by country; in Nigeria the National Industrial Court hears labour disputes.

en.title: Communication and Interpersonal Skills
en.short: Listening, questioning, feedback, assertiveness, conflict and cross-cultural talk in HR conversations.

sections.heading: Listening and questioning
sections.text: Listening is not waiting to speak. Active listening means giving full attention, letting the speaker finish, and checking meaning by summarising. Questioning supports this. Open questions invite detail; closed questions confirm facts; probing questions ask for an example. In an interview, use open questions to explore, then closed questions to verify. In an appraisal, ask the employee to assess their own work first. In a grievance, ask for sequence and specific incidents, not conclusions.

sections.heading: Feedback and assertiveness
sections.text: Feedback should be specific, timely and about behaviour, not personality. Say what was observed and its effect: “The report arrived after the deadline, so the team missed the client meeting.” Ask for their view and agree next steps. Assertiveness means stating your needs or concerns clearly and calmly while respecting the other person. It sits between passive behaviour, where needs are hidden, and aggressive behaviour, where others are ignored. Use short “I” statements: “I need the figures by Thursday.”

sections.heading: Conflict and culture
sections.text: Conflict handling has five common styles: avoiding, accommodating, competing, collaborating and compromising. No style is always best. Collaborating seeks a solution that meets both sides; compromising splits the difference; avoiding may suit a trivial issue. Cross-cultural communication means noticing that directness, silence, eye contact, hierarchy and face-saving can differ. Do not stereotype. Ask how the person prefers to communicate and check your interpretation. In a grievance, separate the people from the problem and focus on facts and future action.

sections.heading: Records and confidentiality
sections.text: HR conversations need records. Case: Amina handles Tunde’s grievance about a supervisor. She listens without interrupting, uses open questions, summarises his account, and agrees a follow-up date. She writes a factual note: date, people, what was said, and agreed actions. Written communication should be clear, brief, accurate and suited to the reader. Confidentiality means sharing personal information only with people who need it, storing it securely, and following the country’s data protection law. Laws differ; check the current official source.

keyPoints: Active listening means giving attention, not interrupting and summarising to check meaning.
Open questions explore, closed questions confirm and probing questions ask for examples.
Feedback should describe specific behaviour and its effect, then invite the employee’s view.
Assertiveness states needs clearly and calmly without ignoring the other person.
Conflict styles include avoiding, accommodating, competing, collaborating and compromising, and the best choice depends on the situation.
In cross-cultural talk, check meanings rather than assume, keep factual records and share personal data only on a need-to-know basis under local law.

en.title: Finance and Accounting for HRM
en.short: Financial statements, budgets, cost concepts, paybill analysis and costing HR proposals.

sections.heading: Statements and budgets
sections.text: Financial statements report a firm’s money. The statement of profit or loss shows income and expenses over a period. The statement of financial position lists assets, liabilities and equity at a date. The statement of cash flows shows cash received and paid. A budget is a plan for a future period, such as a year, and actual results are compared with it to find variances. HR managers use budgets for headcount, pay, training and other people costs. Accounting rules differ by country, so check the local standard.

sections.heading: Cost concepts and paybill
sections.text: Costs are fixed or variable. Fixed costs do not change with output in the short term, such as rent. Variable costs change with output, such as hourly wages or materials. Direct costs can be traced to a product or service; indirect costs cannot. Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost. Labour cost as a proportion of operating cost = total labour cost ÷ total operating cost × 100. Paybill means the total wages and salaries paid to employees. Paybill analysis looks at the total paybill, average cost per employee and paybill as a share of revenue. Example: operating cost 5,000,000 and paybill 1,500,000 give 1,500,000 ÷ 5,000,000 = 30%. With 150 employees, average paybill per employee = 1,500,000 ÷ 150 = 10,000.

sections.heading: Costing and justifying proposals
sections.text: To justify an HR proposal, list all costs: fees, materials, staff time and ongoing costs. Then estimate benefits, such as savings, higher output or lower turnover. Simple cost-benefit reasoning compares them. Net benefit = total benefit − total cost. Benefit-cost ratio = total benefit ÷ total cost. Payback period = initial cost ÷ annual benefit. Example: training costs 200,000 once and is expected to save 80,000 a year for five years. Total benefit = 80,000 × 5 = 400,000. Net benefit = 400,000 − 200,000 = 200,000. Benefit-cost ratio = 400,000 ÷ 200,000 = 2.0. Payback = 200,000 ÷ 80,000 = 2.5 years. Treat estimates with care.

keyPoints: The statement of profit or loss shows performance over a period; the statement of financial position shows assets, liabilities and equity at a date.
A budget is a plan compared with actual results to find variances.
Total cost = fixed cost + variable cost.
Labour cost proportion = total labour cost ÷ total operating cost × 100.
Payback period = initial cost ÷ annual benefit.
Net benefit = total benefit − total cost; benefit-cost ratio = total benefit ÷ total cost.

en.title: Business Ethics and Corporate Social Responsibility
en.short: Ethical theories, stakeholders, CSR, sustainability, governance and fair employment.

sections.heading: Ethical theories
sections.text: Ethics asks what conduct is right. Three standard approaches are useful. Utilitarianism, a consequentialist theory, judges an action by its overall consequences: choose the option that produces the greatest good for the greatest number. Deontology, or duty-based ethics, judges the action itself: some duties, such as telling the truth and respecting persons, bind us whatever the result. Virtue ethics asks what a good person would do, stressing honesty, courage and fairness. These theories can conflict. A manager may cut staff to save the remaining jobs (a utilitarian argument), but this breaks a promise to employees, which deontology condemns.

sections.heading: Stakeholders and CSR
sections.text: Stakeholder thinking says a firm affects and is affected by groups beyond shareholders: employees, customers, suppliers, communities and regulators. Corporate social responsibility (CSR) is the firm’s voluntary concern for these groups and for society, going beyond legal minimums. Sustainability means meeting present needs without harming future generations, often summarised by the triple bottom line: profit, people and planet. A made-up Lagos food firm, Adeyemi Foods, considers closing a costly safety training programme. Stakeholder analysis shows employees face injury, customers face unsafe food, and the firm faces reputational and legal risk.

sections.heading: Governance and employment
sections.text: Corporate governance is the system of rules, board oversight and controls by which a company is directed and held accountable. It covers transparency, audit and checks on power. In employment, ethical expectations include fair pay, safe work, equal treatment, privacy and a voice at work. They also include refusing forced labour and child labour. Governance makes these duties operational through policies, reporting and complaint channels.

sections.heading: Foundation versus profession
sections.text: This topic gives a first-year foundation for all managers. The later professional ethics topic for HR practitioners examines HR’s own codes, confidentiality, dual loyalties and professional judgement in detail.

keyPoints: Utilitarianism judges actions by consequences, deontology by duties, and virtue ethics by character.
Stakeholder thinking considers everyone affected by the firm, not only shareholders.
CSR is voluntary social and environmental responsibility beyond legal minimums.
Sustainability meets present needs without harming future generations, often through the triple bottom line.
Corporate governance provides board oversight, transparency and accountability.
Employment ethics covers fair pay, safety, equal treatment, privacy and voice, while the later professional topic focuses on HR practitioners’ own conduct.

en.title: Strategic Human Resource Management
en.short: How HR practices align with strategy, fit together and affect performance, with contested evidence.

sections.heading: Strategy and fit
sections.text:
Strategic HRM is the planned use of HR policies and practices to help an organisation reach its goals. Vertical fit means HR practices support the business strategy. Horizontal fit means the practices support one another. A firm competing on low cost may stress productivity and tight staffing. A firm competing on service may invest more in selection, training and reward for service quality.

Consider a made-up Lagos retailer, Ada Stores, which chooses fast, friendly service. It links recruitment to service skills, training to customer care, and reward to service quality. If it rewarded only sales volume, horizontal fit would break.

sections.heading: Models and frameworks
sections.text:
Two classic models guide the field. The Michigan matching model treats HR as a means of matching people and practices to strategy. The Harvard model stresses stakeholder interests, HR policy choices and long-term outcomes.

The resource-based view argues that sustained advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and non-substitutable. A skilled, motivated workforce can be such a resource, but only when the whole HR system is difficult to copy.

The AMO framework says performance depends on ability, motivation and opportunity. Ability comes from practices such as selection and training. Motivation comes from reward and appraisal. Opportunity comes from job design and involvement. HR practices should raise all three together.

sections.heading: Performance debate
sections.text:
Some studies report that bundles of high-performance work practices, such as selective hiring, training, employee involvement and performance-related pay, are linked to better performance. Other studies find weak or no effects. The evidence is hard to interpret. Profitable firms may afford more HR, so cause can run backwards. Measures differ, and effects depend on context.

The universalistic view looks for practices that always help. The contingency view says fit with strategy and context matters. The configurational view says bundles of practices matter more than single practices. No single universal effect is established, so claims should be modest and checked against local evidence.

keyPoints: Strategic HRM aligns HR policies and practices with organisational goals.
Vertical fit is alignment with business strategy, while horizontal fit is consistency among HR practices.
The resource-based view sees a valuable, rare and hard-to-imitate people system as a possible source of advantage.
The AMO framework says performance depends on ability, motivation and opportunity.
Evidence linking HRM to performance is mixed and often cannot prove cause.
Contingency and configurational views warn that effects depend on strategy, context and bundles of practices.

en.title: Workforce Planning and HR Forecasting
en.short: Demand and supply forecasts, gap analysis, turnover and absence, and action plans.

sections.heading: Forecasting demand and supply
sections.text: Demand forecasting estimates how many people, with which skills, an organisation will need at a future date. Methods include trend projection from past output, ratios such as staff per patient or per tonne, managerial judgement and the Delphi method, where experts answer rounds of questions. Supply forecasting estimates how many will be available. Internal supply uses staffing tables (headcount by unit and grade), skills inventories and expected losses. External supply depends on the local labour market and the occupation. Country and industry matter, so use current official labour market data.

sections.heading: Gap and flows
sections.text: Gap analysis compares demand with supply. A positive gap is a shortage; a negative gap is a surplus. Two flow measures help. Turnover rate = leavers ÷ average number of employees × 100 over a period. Absence rate = days lost ÷ (employees × working days) × 100. High turnover or absence raises the supply needed. Analyse by department, role, length of service and cause, not only as one total.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A department needs 120 skilled staff next year. It has 100 now, expects 12 leavers and 5 transfers in. Internal supply = 100 − 12 + 5 = 93. Gap = 120 − 93 = 27, a shortage. Turnover = 12 ÷ 100 × 100 = 12%. If 100 staff each have 250 working days and 2,000 days are lost, absence = 2,000 ÷ (100 × 250) × 100 = 8%. The plan must cover 27 people, allowing for training time and further losses.

sections.heading: Action plans and limits
sections.text: For a shortage, plan recruitment, training, redeployment, overtime or contractors. For a surplus, consider a hiring freeze, shorter hours, redeployment, natural turnover and, last, redundancy (job cuts when roles are no longer needed). Redundancy law and consultation duties differ by country, so check the current law. Scenario planning tests best, likely and worst cases, for example demand plus or minus 10%. Forecasts are estimates: assumptions, data quality and labour markets change. Review them regularly and state the uncertainty.

keyPoints: Demand forecasting estimates future staffing needs; supply forecasting estimates available staff.
Gap = demand − supply; positive means shortage, negative means surplus.
Turnover rate = leavers ÷ average employees × 100 for the period.
Absence rate = days lost ÷ (employees × working days) × 100.
Action plans may recruit, train, redeploy, use contractors, freeze hiring or make redundancies, subject to local law.
Scenario planning and regular review help, but forecasts remain uncertain estimates.

en.title: Job Analysis and Job Design
en.short: Methods, descriptions, person specifications, competencies and job design, linked to HR decisions.

sections.heading: Analysis and outputs
sections.text:
Job analysis is the systematic collection of information about a job: its tasks, duties, responsibilities, working conditions and the knowledge, skills and abilities needed. Common methods are observation, interviews, questionnaires, work diaries and the critical incident technique, which records examples of especially good or poor behaviour. Each method has limits, so analysts often combine them.

The main outputs are the job description and the person specification. A job description states the job title, purpose, reporting lines, main duties and conditions. A person specification states the qualifications, experience, skills and attributes required, often split into essential and desirable. It must relate to the job, not to irrelevant personal traits.

sections.heading: Competency and design
sections.text:
A competency framework groups the behaviours and skills the organisation values, with levels showing what good performance looks like. It can cover many roles, while a person specification is written for one vacancy. Frameworks help recruitment, appraisal and development, but they must be fair, observable and reviewed.

Job design decides how work is arranged. Job rotation moves people between tasks. Job enlargement adds similar tasks at the same level. Job enrichment adds responsibility, autonomy and feedback, drawing on the job characteristics model of Hackman and Oldham. Rotation can reduce boredom but may not deepen skill. Enlargement widens work but can feel like more of the same. Enrichment gives more control and meaning, but needs training and trust.

sections.heading: From analysis to decisions
sections.text:
A made-up case: Amina is an HR officer at a logistics firm in Ibadan, Nigeria. She interviews dispatch clerks, observes a shift and checks incident reports. She writes a job description and person specification, then a competency framework for safe loading and customer service. The advert uses the person specification. Job evaluation, which compares roles by factors such as skill and responsibility, uses her analysis to set a fair pay grade. Appraisal uses the duties and competencies as standards.

Good analysis therefore supports recruitment, pay and performance. It must be current, written in plain language and reviewed when jobs change.

keyPoints: Job analysis gathers task and worker information through methods such as observation, interviews and questionnaires.
A job description describes the job; a person specification describes the required person.
Competency frameworks group observable behaviours and skills across roles and levels.
Job rotation moves people between tasks, enlargement adds similar tasks, enrichment adds responsibility and autonomy.
Job analysis outputs feed recruitment criteria, job evaluation for pay and performance standards.
Review job information regularly because roles change.

en.title: Recruitment and Selection
en.short: Recruitment sources, employer branding, selection methods, reliability, validity, adverse impact and legal limits.

sections.heading: Recruitment sources and branding
sections.text:
Recruitment attracts candidates; selection chooses among them. Sources are internal, such as promotions and transfers, or external, such as job boards, referrals, campus visits, agencies and social media. Internal recruitment is cheaper and motivates staff but limits fresh ideas. External recruitment widens the pool but costs more. Methods should reach the right labour market and give honest information.

Employer branding is the image an employer builds as a place to work. A realistic job preview describes good and hard parts of the role, helping candidates self-select and reducing early leaving.

sections.heading: Designing the selection process
sections.text:
Selection design starts from job analysis, which identifies tasks and the knowledge, skills and abilities needed. Criteria must be job-related and agreed before assessment. A common design uses sequential hurdles: application screening, interview, tests and references. Each stage should add information and be applied consistently.

Interviews are most useful when structured: same questions, defined scoring and trained interviewers. Tests may measure cognitive ability, job skills or personality. Assessment centres use several exercises and trained assessors, often for complex or managerial roles.

sections.heading: Reliability, validity and impact
sections.text:
Reliability means consistency: the same candidate should score similarly on repeat or equivalent measures. Validity means the method measures what it claims and predicts job performance. A test can be reliable but invalid.

Adverse impact means one group is rejected more often. In the United States, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission’s Uniform Guidelines use the four-fifths rule. Selection rate is the proportion hired. If the highest rate is 50% and another group’s rate is 30%, the ratio is 30 ÷ 50 = 0.60, below 0.80, so adverse impact may exist. The rule is a guide, not law.

sections.heading: Law and ethics
sections.text:
Legal constraints vary by country. Examples include Title VII of the US Civil Rights Act 1964, the UK Equality Act 2010 and South Africa’s Employment Equity Act 1998. They restrict discrimination and may require reasonable adjustments for disabled candidates.

Data protection law limits applicant records. Ethically, keep selection transparent, avoid irrelevant personal questions and protect confidentiality. Check current local law and official guidance.

keyPoints: Recruitment sources are internal or external; choose methods that fit the labour market and role.
Employer branding and realistic job previews affect applicant quality and early leaving.
Selection criteria should come from job analysis and be applied consistently.
Structured interviews and multiple assessment methods improve selection.
Reliability is consistency; validity is job-relatedness and prediction.
Adverse impact ratio = group selection rate ÷ highest selection rate; the US four-fifths rule uses 0.80, but law varies by country.

en.title: Onboarding, Employee Engagement and Retention
en.short: Induction, socialisation, engagement, retention and voluntary turnover analysis.

sections.heading: Induction and socialisation
sections.text: Induction is the formal start: policies, safety, systems, pay and role duties. Socialisation is the longer process by which a newcomer learns culture, norms, relationships and what success looks like. Good onboarding blends both: a realistic job preview before the start, a buddy or mentor, clear early tasks, and manager check-ins at 30, 60 and 90 days. It reduces early exit and speeds performance.

sections.heading: Engagement and satisfaction
sections.text: Engagement is a positive, work-related state shown by vigour, dedication and absorption, or willingness to give discretionary effort. Job satisfaction is a narrower evaluation: how content someone is with pay, conditions and the job. A satisfied employee may be passive; an engaged one invests energy. Drivers include meaningful work, autonomy, fair reward, recognition, supervisor support, development and voice. Measure with validated surveys such as the Utrecht Work Engagement Scale, pulse surveys, focus groups and exit data. Compare by team and over time, not by one score.

sections.heading: Retention and turnover
sections.text: Retention means keeping valued employees and reducing avoidable voluntary exits. Stable headcount is not enough: people may leave and be replaced, or key talent may go while numbers look unchanged. Strategies include realistic recruitment, good onboarding, fair pay, career paths, flexible work, recognition, good managers, stay interviews and action on survey results. Analyse voluntary turnover separately from involuntary. Calculate rate = voluntary leavers ÷ average headcount × 100. Also examine tenure, function, performance and reasons.

sections.heading: Worked turnover example
sections.text: Example: opening headcount 190, closing 210, average = (190 + 210) ÷ 2 = 200. Voluntary leavers 24, involuntary 6. Voluntary turnover = 24 ÷ 200 × 100 = 12%. Total turnover = 30 ÷ 200 × 100 = 15%. If 8 voluntary leavers were high performers, dysfunctional voluntary rate = 8 ÷ 200 × 100 = 4%. Headcount rose by 20, yet 12% chose to leave; retention needs the breakdown, not just the closing number.

keyPoints: Onboarding combines formal induction with longer socialisation into the culture and relationships.
Engagement is a positive work state of vigour, dedication and absorption, not merely job satisfaction.
Job satisfaction is an evaluation of the job and conditions; a satisfied employee need not be engaged.
Retention means keeping valued employees and reducing avoidable voluntary exits, not just holding headcount steady.
Voluntary turnover rate = voluntary leavers ÷ average headcount × 100.
Average headcount = (opening headcount + closing headcount) ÷ 2, and turnover should be analysed by performance, tenure and reasons.

en.title: Learning, Training and Development
en.short: Training needs, learning theories, methods, transfer and Kirkpatrick evaluation, plus development planning.

sections.heading: Three related terms
sections.text:
Training builds skills for the current job. Development prepares a person for wider or future responsibilities. Education gives general knowledge and reasoning not tied to one job. They overlap, but HR plans training for a specific gap and development for a career path.

Case: at a made-up Kenyan bank, tellers are trained on a new cash system. A promising teller joins a development plan with mentoring and a budgeting course. The cash system training serves the current job; the mentoring and the course prepare the teller for future roles.

sections.heading: Needs and learning
sections.text:
Training needs analysis (TNA) finds gaps before design. Organisational analysis asks where training supports strategy. Task analysis lists what a job requires. Person analysis identifies who lacks what. TNA uses performance data, job analysis and employee views.

Theories guide design. Behaviourism stresses practice and feedback. Cognitivism focuses on memory and understanding. Social learning theory, from Albert Bandura, says people learn by observing models. Experiential learning, from David Kolb, cycles through experience, reflection, thinking and testing. Andragogy, from Malcolm Knowles, says adults need relevance and problem-centred learning.

sections.heading: Methods and transfer
sections.text:
Methods include on-the-job coaching, job rotation and apprenticeships, and off-the-job lectures, case studies, simulations and e-learning. Choose by cost, risk, learner numbers and skill. Practical skills need practice; attitudes need discussion and role play.

Transfer of learning means applying training at work. It improves when tasks are realistic, managers give feedback, and barriers are removed. Near transfer repeats the trained task closely; far transfer applies principles to new situations.

sections.heading: Evaluation and planning
sections.text:
Kirkpatrick’s four levels are reaction, learning, behaviour and results. Reaction asks if learners liked the training. Learning checks knowledge or skill gains. Behaviour checks whether work behaviour changed. Results checks outcomes such as errors, sales or safety. A happy reaction does not prove learning.

Development planning turns goals into actions. Individual development plan names the target, actions, support and review date. The 70-20-10 model suggests much learning comes from experience, some from others and some from courses, but treat it as a guide, not a rule.

keyPoints: Training is job-focused; development is future-focused; education is broader general knowledge.
Training needs analysis examines organisation, task and person levels before design.
Behaviourism, cognitivism, social learning, experiential learning and andragogy offer different design principles.
Training methods should match the skill, risk, cost and number of learners.
Transfer of learning needs realistic practice, manager support and removal of workplace barriers.
Kirkpatrick’s four levels are reaction, learning, behaviour and results; a positive reaction alone does not prove learning.

en.title: Performance Management
en.short: Goal setting, standards, appraisal methods, feedback, rating errors, improvement plans and continuous review.

sections.heading: Continuous process, not event
sections.text:
Performance management is the continuous cycle of planning, monitoring, reviewing and improving performance. It includes regular check-ins, goal adjustment and feedback during the year.

An annual appraisal is a single formal event, often a yearly rating meeting. The appraisal is one tool inside performance management, not the whole system. Treating the appraisal as the only activity weakens trust and delays action.

sections.heading: Goals and standards
sections.text:
A goal is a desired result to reach by a date. A performance standard is the expected level of quality, quantity, time or behaviour in the job. Good goals are SMART: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant and time-bound.

Standards make expectations concrete. For example, a customer service officer in a Lagos bank may have the goal of cutting complaint response time from 48 to 24 hours by 30 June. Her standards require answering calls within three rings and logging every complaint.

sections.heading: Appraisal and feedback
sections.text:
Appraisal methods include rating scales, critical incident records (brief notes of specific good or poor work events), essays, behaviourally anchored rating scales (BARS) and 360-degree feedback. BARS links ratings to examples of behaviour. 360-degree feedback collects views from managers, peers, subordinates and sometimes customers.

Feedback works best when it is timely, specific, behavioural and two-way. It should describe what happened and its effect, not attack the person. A short check-in after a task teaches more than a comment written months later.

sections.heading: Rating errors and improvement
sections.text:
Rating errors distort judgement. Halo effect lets one good trait colour every rating; horns effect does the opposite. Leniency (over-generous scores), strictness (over-harsh scores), central tendency (clustering at the middle) and recency bias (over-weighting recent events) also skew scores.

A performance improvement plan (PIP) is a structured document for someone below standard. It states the gap, measurable targets, support, review dates and possible consequences. It must be fair, documented and consistent with policy and local law. In a made-up case, Amina, a Kano sales assistant, misses her target three months running. Her manager agrees a PIP with weekly coaching, a clear weekly target and a four-week review.

keyPoints: Performance management is a continuous cycle; the annual appraisal is only one formal event within it.
Goals should be SMART, and performance standards define the expected level of quality, quantity, time or behaviour.
Appraisal methods include rating scales, critical incident records, BARS and 360-degree feedback.
Feedback should be timely, specific, behavioural and two-way.
Rating errors such as halo, leniency and recency bias distort appraisal judgements.
A performance improvement plan sets measurable targets, support and review dates for below-standard performance.

en.title: Reward Management: Pay, Benefits and Total Reward
en.short: Pay structures, job evaluation, market pay, pay for performance, benefits and total reward.

sections.heading: Pay structures and equity
sections.text: Reward management designs and administers pay and benefits. A pay structure groups jobs into grades and gives each grade a pay range with a minimum, midpoint and maximum. Job evaluation judges the relative worth of jobs inside the organisation, using ranking, classification or points. It supports internal equity: perceived fairness in pay differences between jobs. Internal equity is separate from external competitiveness, which compares pay with the labour market. A structure can be internally fair but fail to attract staff if it is far below market.

sections.heading: Market pay and competitiveness
sections.text: Market pay is the rate for comparable work in the external labour market. HR uses pay surveys and benchmarking, often comparing medians and quartiles. A compa-ratio compares pay with a reference point: compa-ratio = salary ÷ midpoint. Example: a grade ranges from 40,000 to 60,000. Midpoint = (40,000 + 60,000) ÷ 2 = 50,000. Range spread = (60,000 − 40,000) ÷ 40,000 = 50%. An employee paid 45,000 has compa-ratio 45,000 ÷ 50,000 = 0.90. If the market median is 52,000, the midpoint ratio is 50,000 ÷ 52,000 = 0.96. Pay levels and legal rules such as minimum wage, overtime and equal pay vary by country and year, so check current official sources.

sections.heading: Performance, benefits, total reward
sections.text: Pay for performance links part of pay to results through merit pay, bonuses, commissions, piece rates, profit sharing or gain sharing. Motivation links are not automatic. Expectancy theory says effort must lead to performance and performance to a valued reward. Equity theory says people compare pay ratios and may reduce effort if they see unfairness. Agency theory warns that narrow incentives can reward the wrong behaviour. Benefits are indirect rewards such as paid leave, health cover, pensions and allowances; some are statutory, others voluntary. Total reward includes pay, benefits and non-financial rewards such as recognition. Total compensation usually means cash pay plus benefits. Example: base pay 300,000 + bonus 30,000 + employer pension 15,000 + other benefits 45,000 = 390,000.

keyPoints: A pay structure groups jobs into grades with minimum, midpoint and maximum pay.
Job evaluation supports internal equity by judging the relative worth of jobs, not the market rate.
External competitiveness compares pay with market surveys; compa-ratio = salary ÷ midpoint.
Pay for performance can motivate through expectancy and equity, but poor measures can reward the wrong behaviour.
Total reward includes cash pay, benefits and non-financial rewards; total compensation usually means cash pay plus benefits.
Pay levels, minimum wages, overtime and equal pay rules vary by country and year, so check current official sources.

en.title: Employee relations and industrial relations
en.short: Collective bargaining, unions, employee voice, discipline, grievance and dispute resolution.

sections.heading: Unions and bargaining
sections.text: Employee relations is how an employer manages its relationship with employees. Industrial relations usually focuses on collective relations with trade unions, organisations of workers that negotiate together. Collective bargaining is negotiation between employer and union representatives over pay, hours and conditions. In the United Kingdom, bargaining is mostly voluntary, but a union may seek statutory recognition through the Central Arbitration Committee under the Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992. Coverage varies: some countries extend agreements across a sector; others rely on workplace committees.

sections.heading: Voice and participation
sections.text: Employee voice means the channels through which workers influence decisions, such as union representatives, joint consultative committees, staff surveys and suggestion schemes. Participation goes further, giving workers a share in decisions, for example through works councils or worker directors. In the UK, the Information and Consultation of Employees Regulations 2004 require employers with 50 or more employees to inform and consult employees on specified matters when the procedure is triggered. Germany’s works councils and board-level co-determination show a stronger model.

sections.heading: Discipline and grievance
sections.text: Discipline procedures set rules and a fair process for alleged misconduct: investigate, state the case, hold a hearing, allow a companion, decide, and offer an appeal. Grievance procedures let an employee raise a complaint and have it heard, with an appeal. In the UK, the ACAS Code of Practice on Disciplinary and Grievance Procedures sets expected standards; tribunals may adjust awards if an employer unreasonably fails to follow it. Case: a UK warehouse worker accused of repeated lateness is invited to a hearing with a union representative and allowed an appeal.

sections.heading: Resolving disputes
sections.text: Dispute resolution uses negotiation, conciliation, mediation, arbitration or adjudication. Conciliation helps parties reach their own agreement; arbitration imposes a decision. In the UK, ACAS conciliates individual and collective disputes, Employment Tribunals adjudicate legal claims, and the Central Arbitration Committee decides recognition disputes. Collective disputes may lead to industrial action, but legal protection depends on ballots and notice rules. Institutions differ: Nigeria has the National Industrial Court and Labour Act; Germany uses works councils and sectoral bargaining. Check national law.

keyPoints: Collective bargaining is negotiation between employer and union over pay, hours and conditions.
Employee voice can be direct, such as surveys, or indirect, through representatives.
Discipline and grievance procedures should be fair, investigated and allow an appeal.
Conciliation helps parties agree; arbitration imposes a decision.
UK institutions include ACAS, Employment Tribunals and the Central Arbitration Committee; other countries differ.
Legal protection for industrial action depends on following national ballot and notice rules.

en.title: Applied Employment Law for HRM
en.short: Lawful HR procedures for hiring, contracts, pay, hours, discrimination, dismissal and redundancy, with UK examples.

sections.heading: Law and HR role
sections.text:
Employment law sets minimum standards for hiring, managing and ending work. This summary uses the United Kingdom as the named illustration; rules differ in Nigeria and elsewhere, so check local law. UK sources include Acts, regulations, case law and ACAS codes.

HR applies them through contracts, policies and procedures. A non-lawyer may follow clear rules and keep records, but must not give legal advice, interpret uncertain case law or promise a tribunal result. Complex matters go to a qualified lawyer or ACAS.

sections.heading: Hiring, contracts, equality
sections.text:
Recruitment must use objective criteria. UK adverts and questions must not discriminate under the Equality Act 2010, and disabled applicants may need reasonable adjustments. The contract should state pay, hours, holiday, notice and disciplinary and grievance procedures. UK employees and workers must get a written statement of particulars on day one.

Working Time Regulations 1998 normally cap average weekly work at 48 hours unless the worker opts out, and give 11 hours’ daily rest, a 20-minute break after six hours and 28 days’ paid holiday for full-time workers. Minimum wage rates change yearly, so check official rates. The Equality Act 2010 protects nine characteristics, including age, disability, race, sex and sexual orientation, against direct and indirect discrimination, harassment and victimisation.

sections.heading: Dismissal and redundancy
sections.text:
Dismissal needs a fair reason and fair procedure. UK fair reasons include conduct, capability, redundancy, legal restriction and some other substantial reason. The ACAS Code expects investigation, notice of allegations, a meeting, the right to be accompanied and an appeal. Unfair dismissal normally needs two years’ service, but some dismissals are automatically unfair.

Redundancy must be genuine, with fair selection, consultation, notice and statutory pay after two years. Collective consultation applies when 20 or more redundancies are proposed in 90 days. Case: Chidi, a UK HR officer, dismisses Ada for poor performance after warnings, an improvement plan, a hearing and an appeal. If he skips these steps, the dismissal may be unfair.

keyPoints: Employment law sets minimum standards, and HR procedures must apply them consistently.
In the UK, employees and workers must receive a written statement of particulars on day one.
UK working time normally limits average weekly hours to 48 unless the worker opts out.
The Equality Act 2010 protects nine characteristics and covers direct and indirect discrimination, harassment and victimisation.
Fair dismissal needs a fair reason and fair procedure; redundancy needs genuine selection and consultation.
Non-lawyers may apply clear rules but must refer complex matters to qualified lawyers or ACAS.

en.title: Health, safety and employee wellbeing
en.short: Employer safety duties, risk assessment, accident causes, psychosocial hazards and wellbeing.

sections.heading: Duties and risk assessment
sections.text:
Occupational health and safety (OHS) manages risks to physical and mental health arising from work. In most countries the employer has a general duty to provide a safe workplace, consult workers and record and report serious incidents. Exact duties, penalties and enforcement bodies differ by country, so check national law. Enforcement may involve inspectors, notices, fines or prosecution.

Risk assessment is structured: identify hazards, decide who may be harmed and how, evaluate likelihood and severity, apply controls, record and review. Controls follow a hierarchy: eliminate the hazard, substitute something safer, use engineering controls, then administrative controls, and finally personal protective equipment (PPE). PPE is last because it protects only the wearer and depends on correct use.

sections.heading: Accident causation
sections.text: Accidents usually have several causes, not one. The domino theory, associated with H. W. Heinrich, pictures a chain of causes, with an unsafe act or condition as a key link; removing one link can prevent the accident. James Reason’s Swiss cheese model compares defences to slices with holes. Holes open through active failures, such as a mistake, and latent conditions, such as poor design or weak training. When holes line up, harm occurs. Investigation should examine the task, equipment, training, supervision and management system, not blame the injured worker alone.

sections.heading: Psychosocial hazards and wellbeing
sections.text:
Psychosocial hazards are aspects of work design and management that can harm health. Examples include excessive workload, long hours, low control, unclear roles, bullying, harassment and job insecurity. They can cause stress, burnout and absence. Work-life balance means reasonable boundaries between work and personal life. Employers can support it through predictable hours, flexible arrangements, adequate leave and workload control.

Wellbeing programmes may include employee assistance programmes (EAPs), counselling, health screening, mental health training for managers, ergonomics and return-to-work support. Case: a factory notices rising absence in one team. A risk assessment finds short staffing and a shouting supervisor. The employer adds staff, trains the supervisor and offers counselling. Absence falls. Programmes work best when they remove causes of harm, not only individual help.

keyPoints: Employers owe a general OHS duty, but exact legal duties and enforcement differ by country.
Risk assessment identifies hazards and controls them in a hierarchy, with PPE as the last resort.
Accidents usually have multiple causes, including latent management and design failures.
Psychosocial hazards such as overload, low control and bullying harm mental and physical health.
Work-life balance and wellbeing programmes work best when they change work design, not only treat individuals.
Check current national law and involve workers in safety decisions.

en.title: Diversity, Equity and Inclusion
en.short: Diversity dimensions, equality and equity, inclusion, bias, discrimination, accommodation and metrics.

sections.heading: Dimensions and terms
sections.text: Diversity is the mix of differences among people. Dimensions include age, sex, gender identity, race, ethnicity, disability, religion, sexual orientation, nationality, class and education. Some are visible; others are deep-level, such as values and experience. Equality means applying the same rules to everyone. Equity means recognising different starting points and adjusting support so people can compete and contribute fairly. Inclusion means people feel valued, safe to speak and able to influence decisions. A diverse workforce is not automatically inclusive.

sections.heading: Bias and discrimination
sections.text: Unconscious bias is an automatic association that shapes judgement without intent, such as favouring a similar candidate. It is not deliberate prejudice. Discrimination is less favourable treatment because of a characteristic such as sex, race, disability or religion. It can be direct, like refusing to hire a qualified woman, or indirect, where a rule disadvantages a group without good reason. Laws and protected characteristics differ by country. Reasonable accommodation means changing a job, workplace or process so a person with a disability or other need can perform and participate, unless the change causes unjustifiable hardship. Examples are ramps, flexible hours and screen readers. Many countries, including South Africa and the UK, require adjustments, but the legal test varies.

sections.heading: Metrics and cases
sections.text:
Inclusion metrics may track representation by grade, hiring and promotion rates, attrition, pay gaps and accommodation requests resolved. Use several measures, because small numbers and self-reports can mislead. The business case says diverse and inclusive teams may improve decisions, innovation and market insight, but evidence is mixed and context-dependent. The fairness case says people deserve equal concern and respect, and discrimination is wrong even when it costs money. Neither case is settled.

In a made-up case, Ada uses a wheelchair. Equality gives workers the same entrance. Equity provides a ramp. Inclusion means Ada is invited to meetings and her ideas are used. If the ramp costs ₦450,000 and the training budget is ₦1,500,000, it uses 450,000 ÷ 1,500,000 = 30% of that budget.

keyPoints: Diversity is the mix of differences; inclusion is whether people feel valued and able to contribute.
Equality applies the same rules; equity adjusts support for different starting points.
Unconscious bias is automatic and is not the same as deliberate prejudice.
Discrimination can be direct or indirect, and protected characteristics vary by country.
Reasonable accommodation changes the job or workplace unless it causes unjustifiable hardship.
The business case is context-dependent and not settled; the fairness case rests on respect and rights, not only profit.

en.title: Talent Management and Career Development
en.short: Talent reviews, succession planning, career stages and the risks of exclusive talent pools.

sections.heading: Talent management
sections.text: Talent management is the systematic identification, development, deployment and retention of people who are especially valuable to an organisation, either because of current performance or future potential. It is strategic and selective. Routine training builds job-related skills for many or all employees. Performance management sets goals, appraises work and gives feedback. Talent management uses those inputs but adds decisions about who needs accelerated development, key assignments and succession cover.

sections.heading: Talent reviews
sections.text: Talent identification uses evidence: appraisal results, observed work, feedback from several managers and tests where valid. A talent review is a calibrated discussion in which managers compare evidence and agree on labels such as high potential. A common tool is the performance and potential grid, often called the nine-box grid. It plots current performance against estimated potential. The estimate must be explained, because potential is a prediction and can be biased. Reviews should record development actions, not just labels.

sections.heading: Succession and careers
sections.text: Succession planning identifies and develops internal people for key roles. It covers emergency cover and longer-term pipelines. Career stages are broad phases such as early career, mid-career and late career; their timing varies by person and country. Career planning is the individual’s process of setting goals and actions. Career development is the organisation’s support through stretch assignments, mentoring, coaching and learning. Good practice links the two through honest conversations.

sections.heading: Exclusive pool risks
sections.text: An exclusive talent pool can demotivate people left out, create favouritism and reduce diversity. It may also become stale if members are treated as certain successors. In a made-up case, a retailer labels only ten graduate trainees as high potential. Other graduates reduce effort, and the pool lacks experienced store staff. The retailer moves to inclusive talent management: it develops all staff and gives targeted acceleration to some, with clear criteria and reviews.

keyPoints: Talent management is selective and strategic, not routine training or performance management.
Talent reviews combine evidence and calibration to reduce bias.
The nine-box grid compares current performance with estimated potential.
Succession planning prepares internal people for key roles and emergency cover.
Career planning is individual; career development is organisational support.
Exclusive talent pools risk demotivation, bias and lost diversity, so inclusive approaches are safer.

en.title: HR Analytics and Human Resource Information Systems
en.short: HR metrics, data quality, HR information systems, dashboards, people analytics, privacy and prediction limits.

sections.heading: Metrics and evidence
sections.text: An HR metric is a number that measures a workforce process or result, such as turnover, absence, time to fill a vacancy or cost per hire. A set of linked metrics can test an HR decision. For example, if absence rises after a policy change, compare the rate before and after, and check other possible causes. Evidence-based HR means using reliable data, asking what the number shows and what it cannot show, and avoiding decisions based on one figure alone.

sections.heading: Systems and data quality
sections.text: An HR information system (HRIS) stores and processes employee data, from payroll and leave to recruitment and performance. A dashboard displays selected metrics visually for managers. Its value depends on data quality: accuracy, completeness, consistency and timeliness. Poor data produces misleading dashboards. Basic people analytics uses HR and business data with statistics to answer questions, such as whether training reduced turnover. Start with a clear question, define each metric, and check the data before analysing it.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.text: A firm has 200 employees on average. It records 30 leavers in a year. Turnover = 30 ÷ 200 × 100 = 15%. Its recruitment cost was ₦1,200,000 for 12 hires, so cost per hire = 1,200,000 ÷ 12 = ₦100,000. Absence was 400 days lost. With 200 employees and 220 possible working days each, absence rate = 400 ÷ (200 × 220) × 100 = 0.9%, to one decimal place. These figures help compare teams or years, but they need consistent definitions.

sections.heading: Privacy and prediction
sections.text: Data protection law differs by country, for example Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 and the EU GDPR. Collect only necessary data, secure it, limit access and tell employees how it is used. People analytics can predict poorly when data are biased or small, and predictions are probabilities, not certainties. Use analytics to inform judgement, not replace it, and check legal and ethical limits.

keyPoints: An HR metric is a measure of a workforce process or result, such as turnover or cost per hire.
Turnover rate = leavers ÷ average employees × 100.
Cost per hire = total recruitment cost ÷ number of hires.
An HRIS stores and processes employee data; a dashboard displays selected metrics, and its value depends on data quality.
Data protection laws differ by country, so collect only necessary data, secure it and limit access.
People analytics supports judgement but predictions are uncertain, especially with biased or small data.

en.title: International and Comparative HRM
en.short: Multinational staffing, expatriation, localisation and comparative employment systems.

sections.heading: Multinational HRM
sections.text: International HRM is the management of people across national borders. A multinational corporation (MNC) operates in more than one country and must adapt HR policies to local law, labour markets and customs while keeping a common strategy. It faces tension between consistency and local responsiveness. For example, a head office may set global ethics standards, but pay, leave and dismissal rules must follow each host country. Institutions differ: employment law, unions and social security are shaped by national and regional rules, so no single HR model fits every country.

sections.heading: Staffing and expatriation
sections.text: Global staffing choices include ethnocentric (parent-country staff in key posts), polycentric (host-country staff) and geocentric (best person regardless of nationality). An expatriate is an employee sent to work in another country, usually on a fixed assignment. Expatriation can transfer knowledge but is costly and can fail when family adjustment or culture shock is ignored. Localisation means replacing expatriates with local staff over time. In a made-up case, a Nigerian bank opens a subsidiary in Ghana. It sends manager Chidi from Lagos for two years to set up systems, then promotes Ghanaian deputy Ama into the role. This balances control with local knowledge.

sections.heading: Comparative employment systems
sections.text: Comparative HRM studies how employment systems differ between countries. These systems include labour law, collective bargaining, training and welfare. The varieties of capitalism approach distinguishes liberal market economies, where firms rely more on markets, from coordinated market economies, where institutions support long-term cooperation. The labels are broad and debated. A student should check the actual rules in each country rather than assume a model.

sections.heading: Cross-cultural management
sections.text: Cross-cultural management is the study of how cultural differences affect work. Hofstede’s dimensions, such as individualism and power distance, are widely taught but criticised for treating cultures as uniform. Use them as questions, not labels. Training can prepare staff for overseas work, but it cannot remove the need to learn local practices. Managers should combine cultural awareness with local legal advice and employee consultation.

keyPoints: International HRM balances global consistency with local adaptation.
Ethnocentric, polycentric and geocentric are three global staffing approaches.
An expatriate is sent to work abroad; localisation replaces expatriates with local staff.
Employment law, collective bargaining and welfare institutions differ by country, so check local rules.
Cross-cultural frameworks such as Hofstede’s are useful prompts, not fixed labels.
Expatriate assignments need family and cultural support, not only technical preparation.

en.title: Professional ethics for HR practitioners
en.short: HR codes, confidentiality, fairness, conflicts, whistleblowing and ethical choices in recruitment, pay and discipline.

sections.heading: Codes and compliance
sections.text: Professional codes set expected conduct: integrity, competence and respect. Many HR bodies publish them, for example CIPD in the UK and SHRM in the US; read the current version for your country. A code is guidance, not law. Legal compliance means meeting statutes, regulations and contracts. Ethical judgement asks whether an action is fair, honest and defensible even when lawful. Ethics can demand more than the legal minimum.

sections.heading: Confidentiality and conflicts
sections.text: HR holds pay, health, grievance and investigation records. Keep them confidential: share only with people who need the information, store it securely and follow the data protection law of the country. Confidentiality is not secrecy at all costs; legal or safety exceptions may require disclosure. A conflict of interest arises when personal interest could affect judgement. Declare it and step aside. Case: an HR officer interviewing her cousin should tell her manager and let another panel member lead.

sections.heading: Fairness in people decisions
sections.text: Fairness means consistent, transparent treatment based on job-related evidence. In recruitment, use the same criteria and record reasons; avoid asking about protected characteristics, such as sex, ethnicity, religion or disability, unless the law allows and the job requires it. In pay, explain how rates are set and correct unexplained gaps. In discipline, hear the employee, gather evidence and apply penalties consistently.
