Case: a manager wants to dismiss a worker for lateness without a hearing. Law may require a fair procedure, and ethics also requires a chance to answer. A lawful process can still be biased.

sections.heading: Whistleblowing and decisions
sections.text: Whistleblowing is reporting wrongdoing, such as fraud or unsafe practice, to someone who can act. Protected disclosure laws, which shield whistleblowers from retaliation, differ by country; a policy may offer confidential internal routes and an external route. Ethical decision making: state the facts, identify stakeholders, check law and the code, weigh duties and consequences, consider alternatives, ask how the decision would look in public, then record it. Case: an HR officer who finds falsified safety training records should preserve evidence and report through the channel, not quietly delete them.

keyPoints: Professional codes guide conduct but do not replace law or personal judgement.
Legal compliance is the minimum; ethical judgement asks whether a lawful action is also fair and defensible.
Keep employee data confidential and share it only with people who need it.
Declare conflicts of interest and step aside from the decision.
Apply consistent, job-related criteria in recruitment, pay and discipline, and hear the employee before penalties.
Whistleblowing channels and protected disclosure laws vary by country; preserve evidence and report wrongdoing properly.

en.title: Research Methods for HRM
en.short: Designing, conducting and critically reading HR research, from sampling to ethics.

sections.heading: Design and evidence
sections.text: Start with a clear research question. Research design is the plan that links question, evidence, methods and analysis. A literature review summarises what is already known, shows the gap and sharpens the question. Search systematically, record sources and appraise studies for method, sample and relevance. Read evidence critically: ask who was studied, how, what was measured and what limits the author admits.

sections.heading: Sampling and tools
sections.text: Sampling selects part of a population to represent the whole. Probability sampling, such as simple random sampling, gives every member a known chance of selection and supports generalisation. Non-probability sampling, such as convenience or purposive sampling, is common in HR but limits generalisation. Questionnaires suit many respondents; keep items clear, pilot them and report response rate. Interviews give depth; semi-structured interviews use a guide and probes. Observation records behaviour in context; declare whether the observer participates. Secondary data, such as HR records or official statistics, is cheap but check definitions, completeness and time period.

sections.heading: Analysis and example
sections.text: Quantitative analysis uses counts, percentages, averages and cross-tabulations. Qualitative analysis codes text into themes, then compares cases. Triangulation uses more than one source or method to strengthen claims. Example: 80 questionnaires are sent and 60 return. Response rate = 60 ÷ 80 = 75%. If 45 respondents are women, that is 45 ÷ 60 = 75% of returns. Report both denominators, because non-response can bias results.

sections.heading: Ethics and planning
sections.text: Research ethics protects people and trust. Seek approval, obtain informed consent, explain voluntary participation, protect anonymity and confidentiality, store data securely and avoid harm. Plan a small project by fixing scope, access, timetable, budget and ethics. Pilot instruments, keep a decision log and state limitations honestly.

keyPoints: A research design links the question, evidence, methods and analysis.
A literature review identifies the gap and justifies the question.
Probability sampling supports generalisation; non-probability sampling limits it.
Response rate = returned questionnaires ÷ questionnaires sent.
Qualitative analysis codes text into themes; quantitative analysis uses counts and percentages.
Ethics require informed consent, confidentiality and no harm.

en.title: Advanced HRM Theory
en.short: Resource-based, institutional, critical and employment-relations views of HRM and its performance link.

sections.heading: Resource-based view
sections.text: The resource-based view (RBV) asks why firms differ. It argues that sustained advantage comes from resources that are valuable, rare, hard to imitate and not easily substituted. Human capital, tacit knowledge and social systems can qualify, but only if they meet those tests. Strategic HRM uses RBV to claim that coherent bundles of practices create firm-specific skills. Critics note that the tests are hard to measure and can become tautological: successful firms are said to have rare resources because they succeeded.

sections.heading: Institutional and critical
sections.text: Institutional theory explains similarity. Coercive, mimetic and normative pressures, called isomorphism, push organisations to adopt accepted HR practices, sometimes for legitimacy rather than efficiency. Critical HRM asks whose interests such practices serve. It treats much HRM as a managerial ideology that stresses unity and hides power, consent and resistance. Both views challenge the strategic HRM assumption that practices are chosen purely for performance.

sections.heading: Employment relations
sections.text: Employment-relations theory is often pluralist. It sees employers and workers as having partly conflicting interests, so voice, collective bargaining and dispute resolution matter. It criticises unitarist HRM for assuming shared goals and for marginalising unions. A critical comparison therefore turns on assumptions: RBV is managerial and performance-led; institutional theory is sociological and legitimacy-led; critical theory is emancipatory; employment relations is collective and conflict-aware.

sections.heading: Performance link
sections.text:
The HRM-performance link is often a black box: practices affect skills, motivation and opportunity (the AMO model), which affect behaviour and then performance. Evidence is mixed. Studies struggle with causality, reverse causality, measurement and context. Strategic HRM often assumes vertical fit with business strategy, horizontal fit among practices, and that workers share management’s goals.

Case: Adom Bank, a fictional Ghanaian bank, introduces teamwork and performance pay. RBV sees rare skilled teams; institutional theory sees a practice copied from rivals; critical theory asks whether staff consent or comply; employment relations asks whether the union was consulted. Each explanation predicts different outcomes.

keyPoints: RBV explains performance differences through valuable, rare, hard-to-imitate and non-substitutable resources.
Institutional theory explains adoption through coercive, mimetic and normative isomorphism and legitimacy.
Critical HRM treats HR practices as managerial ideology shaped by power and consent.
Employment relations is often pluralist and stresses conflicting interests, voice and collective bargaining.
The HRM-performance link is contested because of the black box, causality, measurement and context.
Strategic HRM rests on unitarist and fit assumptions that competing theories question.

en.title: Advanced Research Methods for HRM Dissertations
en.short: Design, measurement, sampling, analysis, mixed methods and ethics for a defensible HRM dissertation.

sections.heading: Design coherence
sections.text:
A master’s dissertation is judged by fit: the research question, philosophical stance, design, sampling, analysis and claims must support one another. A positivist stance usually tests hypotheses with numbers; an interpretivist stance explores meaning; pragmatism supports mixed methods. Justify the choice rather than list methods. A defensible proposal states the question, conceptual framework, design, sampling plan, instruments, analysis plan, ethics and limitations.

Keep the question answerable within your access, time and skills. Show how each method will produce evidence for a specific claim.

sections.heading: Measurement and validity
sections.text:
Measurement assigns numbers or categories to observed properties. Reliability is consistency across items, occasions or raters. Validity is whether an instrument measures the intended construct. HRM constructs such as engagement or performance are often multi-dimensional, so use validated scales where possible, pilot them, and report evidence. Content, construct and criterion validity matter. Common threats include common method bias, where using the same source or method for all measures distorts the results, and social desirability.

Qualitative work uses trustworthiness: credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability. Triangulation, member checking and an audit trail strengthen it.

sections.heading: Sampling and analysis
sections.text:
Probability sampling supports statistical generalisation; non-probability sampling may be justified by access. Justify sample size. Cochran’s formula for a proportion is n0 = z²p(1−p) ÷ e². For 95% confidence, z = 1.96, p = 0.5 and e = 0.05: n0 = 1.96² × 0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 0.05² = 384.16, so about 385. For a population N = 1,200, the finite correction gives n = 385 ÷ (1 + 384 ÷ 1,200) = 292, rounded.

Quantitative analysis uses descriptive and inferential statistics, checking assumptions. Qualitative analysis uses coding and thematic analysis with an audit trail. Mixed methods must justify integration, for example an explanatory sequential design, where a qualitative phase follows the quantitative one to help explain its results.

sections.heading: Ethics and proposal
sections.text: Ethics approval, informed consent, confidentiality, anonymity and secure data storage are required. Workplace research needs care with power relations and vulnerable participants. Follow the data protection law of the country where you collect data. A defensible proposal shows feasibility, timeline, risks and reflexivity.

keyPoints: A defensible proposal aligns question, philosophy, design, sampling, analysis and claims.
Reliability is consistency; validity is whether an instrument measures the intended construct.
Cochran’s formula: n0 = z²p(1−p) ÷ e²; with 95% confidence, p = 0.5 and e = 0.05, n0 ≈ 385.
Finite population correction: n = n0 ÷ (1 + (n0 − 1) ÷ N).
Qualitative quality uses credibility, transferability, dependability and confirmability.
Mixed methods need a stated integration logic, and ethics approval is required before data collection.

en.title: People Analytics and Artificial Intelligence in HRM
en.short: Advanced people analytics, predictive models, AI recruitment and monitoring, bias, transparency and data governance.

sections.heading: Prediction, not certainty
sections.text: People analytics is the systematic use of workforce data to inform decisions. Predictive modelling uses statistical or machine learning methods to estimate the probability of an outcome, such as turnover or absence. Machine learning (ML) is a set of methods that learn patterns from data. Algorithmic decision making means rules or models rank, score or recommend people. Prediction is probabilistic and context-bound: a model trained in one firm or country may not transfer. Correlation is not causation. Ask what decision the model will change and what an error would cost.

sections.heading: AI in hiring and monitoring
sections.text: AI means computer systems that perform tasks associated with human intelligence, such as pattern recognition. In recruitment, AI can screen CVs, rank applicants, run chatbots or analyse interviews. In monitoring, it can track productivity, location or communication. These tools can speed work but may encode historical bias or measure proxies. Human review and job-related validation are essential. Monitoring must respect privacy and worker dignity.

sections.heading: Bias and transparency
sections.text: Algorithmic bias is systematic unfairness in model outputs. It can enter through biased training data, proxy variables such as postcode standing in for ethnicity, labels that reflect past decisions, or optimisation targets. Transparency means disclosing that a model is used, its purpose and its limits. Explainability means giving reasons a person can understand. Legal limits vary: the EU GDPR restricts some solely automated decisions, and the EU AI Act treats some employment uses as high-risk; Nigeria’s Data Protection Act 2023 and South Africa’s POPIA impose data duties. Check current law.

sections.heading: Governance and worked check
sections.text: Data governance covers lawful basis, data quality, retention, security, access and accountability. Validate models on local data, test fairness across groups, document assumptions and keep human oversight. Worked example: 1,000 employees; a model flags 100 as high flight risk. Of these, 30 leave. Of the 900 not flagged, 60 leave. Precision = 30 ÷ 100 = 30%. Recall = 30 ÷ 90 = 33.3%. Accuracy = (30 + 840) ÷ 1,000 = 87%. High accuracy hides poor recall: 60 leavers were missed. Use such checks before acting.

keyPoints: People analytics uses workforce data to inform decisions; predictive models estimate probabilities, not certainties.
Algorithmic decision making can rank or score people, so job-related validation and human review are required.
Bias can enter through training data, proxy variables and labels; test fairness across groups.
Transparency and explainability mean telling people a model is used and giving understandable reasons.
Data governance covers lawful basis, quality, retention, security and accountability.
Precision = true positives ÷ all flagged; recall = true positives ÷ all actual positives; accuracy alone can mislead.

en.title: Sustainable HRM and Decent Work
en.short: Sustainable HRM, decent work, labour standards, supply-chain governance and the efficiency-wellbeing tension.

sections.heading: Sustainable HRM and decent work
sections.text: Sustainable HRM means managing people so that economic performance, social fairness and environmental limits are considered together. It asks whether HR practices can be renewed over time without exhausting workers or communities. Decent work, as the International Labour Organization (ILO) describes it, combines productive work with fair income, safety, social protection, voice and equality. Sustainable HRM supports decent work through fair pay, health and safety, learning and employee voice. But the term can be used loosely: some firms report social projects while keeping insecure contracts. Critical scholars call this weak sustainability when it leaves business goals unchallenged.

sections.heading: Labour standards and governance
sections.text: Labour standards are rules on wages, hours, safety, child labour, forced labour, discrimination and freedom of association. They come from national law, collective agreements and international instruments such as ILO conventions. Enforcement varies by country: some have strong inspectorates, others weak capacity or large informal sectors. In supply chains, brands use codes of conduct, supplier audits, certifications and human rights due diligence, meaning finding, preventing and accounting for harm. The UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights expect firms to respect rights, but they are not a global law. Audits can miss hidden subcontracting and retaliation. Worker voice and grievance channels matter.

sections.heading: Efficiency and wellbeing
sections.text: Efficiency seeks more output per hour or lower cost. Wellbeing needs safe work, reasonable hours, income security and voice. They can align: stable, healthy workers may be more productive and less absent. They can conflict when cost pressure pushes overtime, precarious contracts or speed-up. HR’s task is to make trade-offs visible, not hide them. In a made-up case, Amina is HR manager at a Nairobi garment exporter that wins a large order. To meet the deadline, managers add compulsory overtime. The brand code limits hours, but the factory fears losing the contract. HR can plan capacity, negotiate delivery dates, consult workers and record hours honestly. If it only disciplines supervisors, the pressure returns.

keyPoints: Sustainable HRM integrates economic, social and environmental goals without exhausting workers.
Decent work combines fair income, safety, social protection, voice and equality.
Labour standards come from national law, collective agreements and ILO conventions, and enforcement varies by country.
Supply-chain governance uses codes, audits and due diligence, but audits can miss hidden labour problems.
Efficiency and wellbeing can align, but cost pressure often creates overtime and insecure work.
Critical perspectives warn that sustainability claims can be weak or cosmetic if business goals are unchallenged.
